channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: The path of least resistance is almost always chosen.
item.description: Defaults significantly increase selection rates, but the magnitude of this effect is highly context-dependent and rarely reaches a consistent 90% across different types of decisions.

item.title: Your mood determines your assessment of objective risk.
item.description: The affect heuristic leads you to perceive risks as lower when you are in a positive state.

item.title: You find it nearly impossible to ignore what you know.
item.description: The curse of knowledge describes a cognitive bias where individuals are unable to ignore their own knowledge when predicting how others perceive a situation.

item.title: Your decision quality deteriorates throughout the long workday.
item.description: A 2011 analysis of 1,100 judicial rulings found that parole approval rates dropped from 65% to zero as the day progressed.

item.title: You devalue future rewards to prioritize immediate, smaller gains.
item.description: A 1981 study found that participants often chose a smaller, immediate reward over a significantly larger reward available after a delay.

item.title: You ignore statistical data for a single compelling story.
item.description: A 1973 study showed that even when given accurate probabilities, participants prioritized specific personality descriptions over general base rates.

item.title: Your motivation increases as you approach a finish line.
item.description: The study using loyalty card stamps to demonstrate the goal gradient effect was conducted by Nunes and Drèze in 2006.

item.title: You can remember events that never actually happened.
item.description: Introducing suggestive information after an event can rewrite your personal memory of the original experience.

item.title: Your best-case scenario is your default timeline for tasks.
item.description: People consistently underestimate the time, costs, and risks of future projects.

item.title: You prefer things simply because you have seen them before.
item.description: Repeated exposure to an item generally increases liking up to an optimal point, after which boredom or habituation typically causes liking to decrease.

item.title: Your first impression of a number dictates your final choice.
item.description: Providing an initial, arbitrary value significantly shifts your estimation of a subsequent, unrelated number.

item.title: You believe a win is due after repeated losses.
item.description: The gambler's fallacy is a recognized statistical bias that has been studied since the 19th century; Tversky and Kahneman (1971) published influential research explaining the cognitive mechanism (the law of small numbers) that causes it.

item.title: You rewrite history to make yourself seem clairvoyant.
item.description: Once an outcome is known, you experience hindsight bias, which makes you overestimate how predictable that event was.

item.title: You mistake repeated headlines for objective reality.
item.description: An availability cascade occurs when a chain of expressed perceptions triggers a public belief through repetitive reinforcement.

item.title: You value things more after working for them.
item.description: Effort justification leads you to increase your valuation of a goal simply because it was difficult to achieve.

item.title: You feel less satisfied when you have many options.
item.description: The paradox of choice shows that an abundance of options often leads to paralysis and regret.

item.title: You believe you are less biased than your peers.
item.description: People consistently rate themselves as less susceptible to cognitive biases than the average person.

item.title: You struggle to use objects in new ways.
item.description: Functional fixedness limits your ability to see new uses for common objects.

item.title: You remember your contributions as disproportionately large.
item.description: Egocentric bias causes you to overstate your personal impact on group outcomes.

item.title: Your performance improves solely because you are watched.
item.description: The Hawthorne effect describes how being observed alters your behavior.

item.title: You rate common risks as rarer than they are.
item.description: The availability heuristic leads you to judge probability based on memory, not data.

item.title: You assume everyone agrees with your private opinion.
item.description: The false consensus effect leads you to overestimate how many people share your beliefs.

item.title: You cannot accurately explain how a zipper works.
item.description: The illusion of explanatory depth causes you to overestimate your understanding.

item.title: You blame your failures on the world around you.
item.description: The self-serving bias refers to the tendency to attribute successes to internal factors and failures to external ones.

item.title: You prioritize vivid information over statistical reality.
item.description: Saliency bias causes you to over-weight information that is visually striking or emotionally charged in your judgments.

item.title: Your brain prefers to avoid thinking deeply.
item.description: The cognitive miser theory suggests that you habitually seek shortcuts to minimize mental effort.

item.title: You struggle to change your mind when you feel threatened.
item.description: System justification theory suggests you defend the status quo even when it works against your own interests.

item.title: You spend money differently depending on where it comes from.
item.description: Mental accounting explains why you treat a $100 windfall differently than $100 from your salary.

item.title: You view your own mistakes as bad luck.
item.description: The claim attributes both halves of the actor-observer asymmetry to the Fundamental Attribution Error.

item.title: You feel an immediate desire for what is forbidden.
item.description: Psychological reactance occurs when you perceive a threat to your freedom of choice.

item.title: You judge strangers as kinder based purely on appearance.
item.description: The halo effect is the tendency for an overall impression of a person to influence your feelings about their character.

item.title: You overestimate how much people notice your minor behaviors.
item.description: The spotlight effect is your tendency to feel that your actions are being observed by everyone.

item.title: You derive your self-worth by comparing yourself to peers.
item.description: Social comparison theory posits that you evaluate your own abilities and opinions by comparing them to others.

item.title: You weight negative information more heavily than positive feedback.
item.description: The negativity bias causes you to focus on threats and failures far more than gains.

item.title: You remember details better if they concern your own personality.
item.description: The self-reference effect demonstrates that information encoded in relation to the self is often recalled more effectively than information processed through structural or semantic tasks.

item.title: You are less likely to help someone if you are in a crowd.
item.description: The bystander effect demonstrates that the presence of others reduces your perceived personal responsibility to intervene.

item.title: You remember past events more fondly than you felt them at the time.
item.description: Rosy retrospection is the tendency to assign more positive attributes to past experiences as they fade from memory.

item.title: You assume you are less likely than others to experience misfortune.
item.description: The optimism bias is your tendency to believe that your future will be more positive than the evidence supports.

item.title: You fail to see clear objects when your focus is locked.
item.description: Inattentional blindness describes your inability to perceive visible stimuli when your attention is directed elsewhere.

item.title: You become more likable after making a small, visible mistake.
item.description: The pratfall effect suggests that a minor error makes a highly competent individual more appealing, but can decrease the appeal of someone perceived as mediocre.

item.title: You exaggerate the importance of your current life focus.
item.description: The focusing illusion occurs when you place too much weight on one aspect of life while ignoring others.

item.title: You mistake easy thinking for the truth.
item.description: Cognitive fluency is the phenomenon where you evaluate information as more truthful if it is easy to process.

item.title: Your choice changes based on how the risk is framed.
item.description: The framing effect, as demonstrated by Tversky and Kahneman (1981), shows that people react to choices differently depending on whether they are presented as gains or losses.

item.title: You assume the worst when others act neutrally.
item.description: Hostile attribution bias causes people to interpret ambiguous social cues as intentionally aggressive.

item.title: You work less when you are in a group.
item.description: Latané, Williams, and Harkins (1979) demonstrated social loafing by measuring tasks like shouting and clapping to isolate motivational loss from coordination loss.

item.title: A small favor makes you say yes to big ones.
item.description: The foot-in-the-door technique increases compliance by securing a small, trivial commitment before asking for a substantial one.

item.title: You judge objects as more valuable if they are scarce.
item.description: The scarcity heuristic leads people to place a higher value on items that are perceived as rare or difficult to obtain.

item.title: Asking if you will act makes you more likely to.
item.description: The mere measurement effect describes a phenomenon where measuring intentions may influence subsequent behavior, though this effect is highly context-dependent.

item.title: Your judgment is skewed by what you saw before.
item.description: The contrast effect describes how the perception of an object is changed by its comparison to a preceding object, a phenomenon explored in social psychology regarding attractiveness judgments.

item.title: You are terrible at predicting your feelings in a cold state.
item.description: The hot-cold empathy gap prevents you from accurately anticipating how you will behave when you are hungry, angry, or excited.
